rv.q: So very much of what happens in this production’s ephemeral pools of light feels uncannily like life itself, unaccommodating and bewildering, utterly familiar and gloriously inexplicable.
Man From Nebraska is a dazzler – a great show.
Birney is marvelous to watch as this decent man struggles to find his moral footing in a strange new landscape.
The lengthy delay seems inexplicable, even if the thoughtful but problematic work will probably deeply divide audiences.
But boy, does this play ever need both Birney and Cromer.
That's a perfectly juicy theme, but Letts makes it less a shocking journey to enlightenment than a dutiful stroll round the block.
At Second Stage, in Cromer’s hands and with Birney inhabiting the title role, Man from Nebraska is first-rate drama in a compelling production.
He achieves more devastating effects by tightening his focus onto one Man adrift.
Letts miraculously plucks planetary unitary from one man's spiritual discord.
What might have been clichéd or overly familiar in his hands becomes something extraordinarily new and moving.
Birney's performance is exceptional and jarring as this character who exudes respectfully low-key masculinity is now bent over in tears.
The production remains engrossing, and often deeply moving, throughout.

There is a startling freshness here. None of the characters are stereotypes...Just the bite of true emotion and the message that no matter how lost someone is, there is always someone waiting to find them.
The play is getting a splendid production at Second Stage with an ensemble that’s heaven-sent.
It’s not in the same league as Letts’ “August: Osage County,” to be sure, but any play that makes us consider what being human really means deserves a devoted audience.
A combination of Letts' astute writing and Birney's sympathetic performance never allows us to completely discount his feelings, mired in privilege though they may be.

Those playgoers with the patience for the deliberately slow pace of the Second Stage production of Man from Nebraska will be confirmed in their belief in the power of theatrical mastery...
But for all its humanity and wit, Letts’s play ends up feeling rather schematic under David Cromer’s polished direction.
The idea is provocative, even if it’s completely unpersuasive.

Viewed as a total picture, Man from Nebraska turns out to be riddled with the wrong kind of questions - not the big ones a great playwright asks us, but the niggling little ones that we want to ask the playwright.
Letts’ insightful writing in the play’s barroom scenes between Ken and Tamyra, however, is much more sustained and belongs in another league.
Letts raises a provocative idea but fails to follow through. And when a play turns this hollow even a fine ensemble doesn't have a prayer.
One of the striking things about Letts’s drama is the way it sneaks up on you.

And Tracy Letts’ 2004 play, Man from Nebraska, making its NYC debut at the Second Stage, should be left to its reveals, because ideally you shouldn’t know what’s coming any more than Ken and Nancy will.
Under David Cromer’s direction, however, the silences and ambiguities in the script reflect the characters’ struggles with moral choices that carry considerable weight.
Tony winner Birney (The Humans, Casa Valentina) gives a layered exploration of the complexities of being a regular guy who's just not sure what happened to his life, how he got here.
"Man From Nebraska" is not Tracy Letts' most thought-provoking or exciting play, and there have been better dramas about confused protagonists trying to figure things out for themselves.
But the strong performances and the evocative direction only leave the audience wondering what was the point of the play they had just experienced.

However, once Letts (so successful with August: Osage County ) sets up his situation, he doesn't follow through with characters or situations sufficiently capable of avoiding the mantle of contrivance.
I predict that you will have a strong reaction to the play. Whether it will be negative or positive is the question.

cn.t: Critics praise Reed Birney's exceptional performance and David Cromer's direction in this midlife crisis drama, though reactions split on Letts' slow-burn pacing and episodic structure—some find it masterly and moving, others see it going in circles.
